body: Petiveria alliacea, milled, in a vegan capsule. The ingredient line names the plant and the shell and nothing else.
It does not say which part of the plant. Root and leaf are both milled and sold under this name.
One capsule, or two, with a meal, and at least 500 ml of water.
The listing gives a range rather than a number. Pick the one you are going to take and stay on it.

body: The part of the plant, and the milligrams in a capsule.

The listing also prints two supply figures, 40 days at one a day and 20 at two, that do not agree with its own count of 50 capsules. Both sets are on the sheet below, because one of them is wrong and we do not yet know which.
Dry, out of direct sun, lid on. It does not need a fridge. The powder smells strongly of garlic, so a lid that seals is worth more here than on most jars.
Not for children, and not in pregnancy or breastfeeding.
If you take prescribed medication, particularly a blood thinner, or you have an operation booked, ask your GP or pharmacist before you start.

ingredients.intro: A one ingredient list is a short section. Here is the plant, what the listing says about where it was grown, the part of it that is not named, and the shell it goes into.

cards.p: A slender perennial herb of tropical America and the Caribbean, in a small family long grouped with the pokeweeds. Leaf and root smell strongly of garlic when they are crushed, which is where the species name alliacea comes from, and it carries into the breath of anyone taking it.

cards.alt: Bark and root pieces at the edge of a painted nebula
cards.p: The listing says 100 per cent Petiveria alliacea and does not say which part of it. Root and leaf are both milled in the trade and they are not the same material. Until the label says which, this page will not.

cards.alt: The shop floor at 599 Smithdown Road, shelves along the wall
cards.p: The listing places the harvest in the Caribbean and South America and calls the growing organic. No certifier and no certificate number appear anywhere on it, so read that word as the seller's description rather than as a scheme you can look up.

cards.alt: Plain capsules and a wooden scoop on a slate board, a generated scene
cards.p: The powder goes into a vegan capsule, which is the only other thing the ingredient line names. The shell material itself is not specified. The capsules in this picture are a generated scene rather than a photograph of ours.

ingredients.label: What is on the inside

rows: One ingredient. Petiveria alliacea, milled, in a vegan capsule.
Petiveria alliacea L., family Petiveriaceae, sold in English as anamu and as guinea hen weed. The listing prints the binomial, which is more than most do.
Not printed. The listing says 100 per cent of the plant and never says whether that is root, leaf or both.
The listing names no bulking agent, no binder and no flow agent.
Vegan. The shell material is not named on the listing, so we do not state it here.
50 capsules. There is no milligram figure on the listing. The variant line reads 100 g without saying whether that is powder, filled capsules or the jar, so it is not a strength.

The listing says one a day is a 40 day supply and two a day is a 20 day course. Fifty capsules gives 50 days and 25 days. The two sets of figures do not agree and we have printed both rather than pick the flattering one.
Caribbean and South America, as the listing states. The listing calls the growing organic and names no certifier, so no organic claim is made on this page.
One or two capsules a day with a meal, and at least 500 ml of water. The listing says spring water.
60p a day at one capsule, £1.20 at two, worked from the printed count of 50.
Dry, out of direct sun, lid on. It does not need a fridge. The powder smells of garlic.
None named beyond the capsule shell.
Children. Not in pregnancy or breastfeeding. If you take prescribed medication, particularly a blood thinner, or you have surgery booked, ask your GP or pharmacist before you start.

doctrine.h3: We publish the specification. We do not publish claims about what it does.
doctrine.p: The species is named in Latin, the serving is printed, the price is printed, and the two blanks, part used and milligrams, are printed as blanks. Where the listing contradicts itself on how long a jar lasts, both sets of figures are on the sheet. What anamu does in a person is not something we are permitted to say, so it is not on this page.

reiss.label: From Reiss
reiss.h2: When the arithmetic on a listing does not add up
paras: This listing says 50 capsules at the top, and then says one a day lasts 40 days and two a day lasts 20. Both of those work out at 40 capsules. One of the three numbers is wrong and I do not yet know which, so all three are on the sheet above with that sentence attached.

It matters because the count is the only figure you can use. There are no milligrams on this label, so you cannot compare it with the jar beside it on strength. What you can do is count what arrives, divide the price by it, and hold me to that.

The other blank is the part of the plant. Root and leaf both get milled and sold under this name, and they are not the same thing in a capsule. When the supplier puts it in writing, the row above changes from not printed to whichever it is.
reiss.pull: One of the three numbers on that listing is wrong, so all three are on the sheet.
